claim: Dietary protein absorption in neonatal mammals and fishes relies on the function of a specialized and conserved population of highly absorptive lysosome-rich enterocytes (LREs).
source: Dietary protein absorption in neonatal mammals and fishes relies on the function of a specialized and conserved population of highly absorptive lysosome-rich enterocytes (LREs).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research establishing the role of LREs in protein absorption.

claim: The gut microbiome has been shown to enhance absorption of nutrients, such as lipids, by intestinal epithelial cells.
source: The gut microbiome has been shown to enhance absorption of nutrients, such as lipids, by intestinal epithelial cells.
evidence: This claim references established knowledge about microbiome effects on nutrient absorption.

claim: Microbes slow the pace of protein uptake and degradation in LREs.
source: Using live microscopy-based quantitative assays, we find that microbes slow the pace of protein uptake and degradation in LREs.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from live microscopy assays presented in the manuscript.

claim: Microbes do not affect the number of absorbing LRE cells.
source: While microbes do not affect the number of absorbing LRE cells, microbes lower the expression of endocytic and protein digestion machinery in LREs.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing similar LRE numbers in GF and CV conditions.

claim: Microbes lower the expression of endocytic and protein digestion machinery in LREs.
source: While microbes do not affect the number of absorbing LRE cells, microbes lower the expression of endocytic and protein digestion machinery in LREs.
evidence: This claim is supported by scRNA-seq and HCR data showing reduced expression of endocytic genes in CV conditions.

claim: Some secretory cell types also take up protein and share components of protein uptake and digestion machinery with LREs.
source: We find that microbes affect expression of bacteria-sensing and metabolic pathways in LREs, and that some secretory cell types also take up protein and share components of protein uptake and digestion machinery with LREs.
evidence: This claim is supported by scRNA-seq data showing mCherry uptake in secretory cells.

claim: Impaired protein uptake activity in LREs, along with a protein-deficient diet, alters the microbial community.
source: Impaired protein uptake activity in LREs, along with a protein-deficient diet, alters the microbial community and leads to an increased abundance of bacterial genera that have the capacity to reduce protein uptake in LREs.
evidence: This claim is supported by 16S rRNA gene sequencing data from cubn mutants fed different diets.

claim: Impaired protein uptake activity in LREs leads to an increased abundance of bacterial genera that have the capacity to reduce protein uptake in LREs.
source: Impaired protein uptake activity in LREs, along with a protein-deficient diet, alters the microbial community and leads to an increased abundance of bacterial genera that have the capacity to reduce protein uptake in LREs.
evidence: This claim is supported by 16S sequencing showing increased Aeromonas in cubn mutants and monoassociation experiments showing Aeromonas reduces LRE uptake.

claim: Diet-dependent reciprocal interactions between LREs and the gut microbiome regulate protein absorption.
source: Together, these results reveal that diet-dependent reciprocal interactions between LREs and the gut microbiome regulate protein absorption.
evidence: This claim synthesizes multiple experimental findings showing bidirectional effects between LREs, diet, and microbiome.

claim: Microbiome colonization enhances small intestinal absorption of dietary lipids compared to germ-free animals in zebrafish and mice.
source: In zebrafish and mice, microbiome colonization enhances small intestinal absorption of dietary lipids compared to germ-free (GF) animals (Semova et al., 2012; Martinez-Guryn et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Gut microbiomes increase dietary energy harvest by fermenting complex carbohydrates into short-chain fatty acids that can be absorbed by the gut epithelium.
source: Gut microbiomes are also known to increase dietary energy harvest by fermenting complex carbohydrates into short-chain fatty acids that can be absorbed by the gut epithelium (Cholan et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Drosophila-associated microbes absorb dietary proteins and amino acids and are, in turn, ingested and metabolized by the host, promoting survival under dietary protein-limited conditions.
source: There is evidence that Drosophila-associated microbes absorb dietary proteins and amino acids and are, in turn, ingested and metabolized by the host, promoting survival under dietary protein-limited conditions (Keebaugh et al., 2018; Yamada et al., 2015; Lesperance and Broderick, 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Amino acids secreted by the Drosophila microbiome modify feeding behavior.
source: Furthermore, amino acids secreted by the Drosophila microbiome have been shown to modify feeding behavior (Kim et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Children with kwashiorkor have significantly altered gut microbiomes that promote weight loss when transplanted into GF mice.
source: Children with kwashiorkor, a disease caused by severe protein malnutrition, have significantly altered gut microbiomes that promote weight loss when transplanted into GF mice (Smith et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: LREs are highly endocytic and specialize in the uptake of luminal proteins that they then digest in giant lysosomal vacuoles.
source: Recent work in zebrafish and mice showed that these cells, which we refer to as LREs, are highly endocytic and specialize in the uptake of luminal proteins that they then digest in giant lysosomal vacuoles (Park et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: In mammals, LREs are present only during suckling stages and are lost at weaning.
source: In mammals, LREs are present only during suckling stages and are lost at weaning (Harper et al., 2011), whereas in fishes they are retained through adult life (Park et al., 2019; Noaillac-Depeyre and Gas, 1976; Stroband and Debets, 1978).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: In fishes, LREs are retained through adult life.
source: In mammals, LREs are present only during suckling stages and are lost at weaning (Harper et al., 2011), whereas in fishes they are retained through adult life (Park et al., 2019; Noaillac-Depeyre and Gas, 1976; Stroband and Debets, 1978).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: LREs internalize proteins but not lipids from the intestinal lumen.
source: Using this assay, LREs were shown to internalize proteins but not lipids from the intestinal lumen (Park et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: LREs internalize luminal proteins using an endocytic complex composed of the scavenger receptor cubilin (Cubn), the transmembrane linker amnionless (Amn), and endocytic clathrin adaptor Dab2.
source: LREs internalize luminal proteins using an endocytic complex composed of the scavenger receptor cubilin (Cubn), the transmembrane linker amnionless (Amn), and endocytic clathrin adaptor Dab2 (Park et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Loss of cubilin, amnionless, or Dab2 severely reduces LRE capacity to take up luminal proteins, leading to stunted growth, poor survival, and intestinal edema reminiscent of kwashiorkor.
source: Loss of these components severely reduces their capacity to take up luminal proteins, leading to stunted growth, poor survival, and intestinal edema reminiscent of kwashiorkor (Park et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: LREs are broadly present in vertebrates and likely also in lower chordates.
source: LREs are broadly present in vertebrates and likely also in lower chordates (Nakayama et al., 2019; Yonge, 1923), suggesting LRE development and physiology are ancient and important aspects of intestinal function.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Zebrafish larvae colonized with a complex gut microbiome had electron-dense material in the lysosomes of LREs that was not detected in GF larvae.
source: Specifically, zebrafish larvae colonized with a complex gut microbiome (ex-GF conventionalized or CV) had electron-dense material in the lysosomes of LREs that was not detected in GF larvae (Rawls et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: CV larvae immersed in horse radish peroxidase (HRP) had increased HRP accumulation in LREs.
source: Consistent with these findings, CV larvae immersed in horse radish peroxidase (HRP) had increased HRP accumulation in LREs (Bates et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: GF and CV larvae rapidly took up mCherry in the LREs, absorbing detectable levels of mCherry within 5 min of gavage.
source: We found that GF and CV larvae rapidly took up mCherry in the LREs, absorbing detectable levels of mCherry within 5 min of gavage (Figure 1B-C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B-C.

claim: LREs progressively became more saturated with mCherry between 5–60 min post-gavage in both GF and CV conditions.
source: LREs progressively became more saturated with mCherry between 5–60 min post-gavage in both conditions (Figure 1B-C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B-C.

claim: mCherry fluorescence peaked in the anterior LREs of GF larvae by 40 min PG.
source: However, mCherry fluorescence peaked in the anterior LREs of GF larvae by 40 min PG (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), but the peak did not emerge until 60 min PG in CV larvae (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: mCherry fluorescence peak did not emerge until 60 min PG in CV larvae.
source: However, mCherry fluorescence peaked in the anterior LREs of GF larvae by 40 min PG (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), but the peak did not emerge until 60 min PG in CV larvae (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Between 5 and 60 min PG, the anterior LREs of GF larvae accumulated mCherry at a significantly faster rate than those in CV larvae.
source: Between 5 and 60 min PG, the anterior LREs of GF larvae accumulated mCherry at a significantly faster rate than those in CV larvae (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: GF larvae took up significantly more mCherry than CV larvae by 1 hr PG across the entire LRE region.
source: Across the entire LRE region, GF larvae took up significantly more mCherry than CV larvae by 1 hr PG (Figure 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 1D.

claim: LREs in CV larvae eventually reached a similar level of mCherry uptake to GF larvae by 5 hr PG.
source: However, LREs in CV larvae eventually reached a similar level of mCherry uptake by 5 hr PG (Figure 1E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Luminal mCherry concentrations were equivalent in GF and CV larvae at 1 and 5 hr PG.
source: That did not appear to be the case because luminal mCherry concentrations were equivalent in GF and CV larvae at 1 and 5 hr PG (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), and the microbiome did not degrade mCherry over time (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The microbiome did not degrade mCherry over time.
source: That did not appear to be the case because luminal mCherry concentrations were equivalent in GF and CV larvae at 1 and 5 hr PG (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), and the microbiome did not degrade mCherry over time (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: GF larvae took up significantly more Lucifer Yellow than CV larvae by 1 hr PG.
source: GF larvae took up significantly more LY than CV larvae by 1 hr PG (Figure 1F) but accumulated similar amounts by 3 hr PG (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 1F.

claim: GF and CV larvae accumulated similar amounts of Lucifer Yellow by 3 hr PG.
source: GF larvae took up significantly more LY than CV larvae by 1 hr PG (Figure 1F) but accumulated similar amounts by 3 hr PG (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Microbial colonization reduces the rate of endocytosis in the LRE region.
source: These results suggest that microbial colonization reduces the rate of endocytosis in the LRE region.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental data showing slower uptake kinetics in CV larvae.

claim: A microbial density of 3×10^5 CFU/mL in the GZM was not sufficient to reduce mCherry uptake in CV larvae at 1 hr PG.
source: At 1 hr PG, mCherry uptake was not reduced in CV larvae when the density was 3×105 CFU/mL in the gnotobiotic zebrafish media (GZM) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: A microbial density of 3×10^6 CFU/mL in the GZM was sufficient to significantly reduce mCherry uptake in CV larvae compared to GF larvae.
source: However, a higher density of 3×106 CFU/mL in the GZM was sufficient to significantly reduce mCherry uptake in CV larvae compared to GF larvae (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: mTurquoise degraded over the 1 hr imaging time course in both GF and CV larvae.
source: In both GF and CV larvae, mTurquoise degraded over the 1 hr imaging time course (Figure 2B-C), with the degradation process occurring at a significantly faster rate in GF compared to CV LREs (Figure 2D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B-C.

claim: mTurquoise degradation occurred at a significantly faster rate in GF compared to CV LREs.
source: In both GF and CV larvae, mTurquoise degraded over the 1 hr imaging time course (Figure 2B-C), with the degradation process occurring at a significantly faster rate in GF compared to CV LREs (Figure 2D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The microbiome reduces the rate of cargo uptake and lysosomal protein degradation in LREs.
source: Together, these uptake and degradation kinetics assays demonstrate that the microbiome reduces the rate of cargo uptake and lysosomal protein degradation in LREs.
evidence: This claim synthesizes experimental findings from uptake and degradation assays.

claim: Clustering analysis revealed seventeen cell clusters, including two LRE clusters.
source: Clustering analysis with Seurat (Satija et al., 2015) revealed seventeen cell clusters, including two LRE clusters (Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by scRNA-seq data analysis shown in Figure 3B.

claim: fabp6 expression is highest in the ileocytes, but expression was also detected in the anterior LRE region.
source: Using transgenic reporters, previous studies showed that fabp6 expression is highest in the ileocytes, but expression was also detected in the anterior LRE region (Wen et al., 2021; Lickwar et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The dataset includes 131 GF and 199 CV anterior LREs, along with 359 GF and 381 CV posterior LREs.
source: In total, this dataset includes 131 GF and 199 CV anterior LREs, along with 359 GF and 381 CV posterior LREs (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim reports the cell counts from the scRNA-seq dataset.

claim: GF and CV larvae had proportionally similar numbers of cells in each cluster, including LREs, with the exception of Cloaca 3.
source: GF and CV larvae had proportionally similar numbers of cells in each cluster, including LREs (Figure 3—figure supplement 1), with the exception of a cluster we called Cloaca 3, which was only present in the CV condition (Figure 3D).
evidence: This claim is supported by scRNA-seq data analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1 and Figure 3D.

claim: Cloaca 3 cluster was only present in the CV condition.
source: GF and CV larvae had proportionally similar numbers of cells in each cluster, including LREs (Figure 3—figure supplement 1), with the exception of a cluster we called Cloaca 3, which was only present in the CV condition (Figure 3D).
evidence: This claim is supported by scRNA-seq data analysis shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Cloaca 3 consisted of IECs that are enriched in pathways related to host defense, response to bacteria, and iron ion transport.
source: GO term analysis revealed that Cloaca 3 consisted of IECs that are enriched in pathways related to host defense, response to bacteria, and iron ion transport (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by GO term analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Several genes involved in bacterial response were top cluster markers for Cloaca 3.
source: Several of the genes involved in bacterial response were top cluster markers for Cloaca 3 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by scRNA-seq data analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The development of Cloaca 3 cells is stimulated by the microbiome and functions in microbial sensing and immune response.
source: These results suggest that the development of Cloaca 3 cells is stimulated by the microbiome and functions in microbial sensing and immune response.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that Cloaca 3 only appears in CV conditions and expresses immune-related genes.

claim: There is not a significant difference in the number of active LREs between GF and CV larvae.
source: This experiment revealed that there is not a significant difference in the number of active LREs between GF and CV larvae (Figure 3E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 3E.

claim: The development of most intestinal cell clusters, including LREs, is not dependent on the gut microbiome.
source: Together, these data show that the development of most intestinal cell clusters, including LREs, is not dependent on the gut microbiome.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that most clusters appear in similar proportions in GF and CV conditions.

claim: mCherry is internalized by several cell types in addition to LREs, including ileocytes, goblet, acinar, enteroendocrine, immune, and best4/otop2 cells in both GF and CV conditions.
source: Surprisingly, scRNA-seq analysis revealed that mCherry is internalized by several cell types in addition to LREs (Figure 4A–B). While LREs had the highest percentage of mCherry-positive cells, other mCherry-positive cell types included ileocytes, goblet, acinar, enteroendocrine, immune, and best4/otop2 cells in both GF and CV conditions (Figure 4C).
evidence: This claim is supported by scRNA-seq data analysis shown in Figure 4A-C.

claim: Anterior enterocytes, pharynx, and cloaca clusters contained extremely low levels of mCherry-positive cells.
source: Notably, anterior enterocytes, pharynx, and cloaca clusters contained extremely low levels of mCherry-positive cells (Figure 4C), showing that these cell types have very low protein uptake activity.
evidence: This claim is supported by scRNA-seq data analysis shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The gut microbiome increased the proportions of mCherry-positive cells in several clusters.
source: The gut microbiome increased the proportions of mCherry-positive cells in several clusters (Figure 4D).
evidence: This claim is supported by scRNA-seq data analysis shown in Figure 4D.

claim: The gut microbiome increased the proportion of mCherry-positive enteroendocrine cells by 25%.
source: This effect could be observed in secretory cells such as enteroendocrine, goblet cells, and acinar cells, which increased by 25%, 11%, and 8%, respectively.
evidence: This claim is supported by scRNA-seq data analysis.

claim: The gut microbiome increased the proportion of mCherry-positive goblet cells by 11%.
source: This effect could be observed in secretory cells such as enteroendocrine, goblet cells, and acinar cells, which increased by 25%, 11%, and 8%, respectively.
evidence: This claim is supported by scRNA-seq data analysis.

claim: The gut microbiome increased the proportion of mCherry-positive acinar cells by 8%.
source: This effect could be observed in secretory cells such as enteroendocrine, goblet cells, and acinar cells, which increased by 25%, 11%, and 8%, respectively.
evidence: This claim is supported by scRNA-seq data analysis.

claim: The gut microbiome increased the proportion of mCherry-positive neurons by 13%.
source: The gut microbiome also increased the proportion of mCherry-positive neurons by 13%.
evidence: This claim is supported by scRNA-seq data analysis.

claim: The proportion of mCherry-positive anterior LREs was 84% in GF and 91% in CV conditions.
source: Notably, the proportion of mCherry-positive anterior (84–91%) and posterior (98–97%) LREs was extremely high in both GF and CV conditions, respectively (Figure 4C).
evidence: This claim is supported by scRNA-seq data analysis shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The proportion of mCherry-positive posterior LREs was 98% in GF and 97% in CV conditions.
source: Notably, the proportion of mCherry-positive anterior (84–91%) and posterior (98–97%) LREs was extremely high in both GF and CV conditions, respectively (Figure 4C).
evidence: This claim is supported by scRNA-seq data analysis shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Anterior LREs had a slightly higher proportion of mCherry-positive cells in the CV condition (7% increase).
source: However, the gut microbiome had mixed effects on the number of mCherry-positive LREs. While anterior LREs had a slightly higher proportion of mCherry-positive cells in the CV condition (7% increase), microbes caused a small decrease in the proportion of mCherry-positive posterior LREs (1% decrease) (Figure 4C–D).
evidence: This claim is supported by scRNA-seq data analysis shown in Figure 4C-D.

claim: Microbes caused a small decrease in the proportion of mCherry-positive posterior LREs (1% decrease).
source: However, the gut microbiome had mixed effects on the number of mCherry-positive LREs. While anterior LREs had a slightly higher proportion of mCherry-positive cells in the CV condition (7% increase), microbes caused a small decrease in the proportion of mCherry-positive posterior LREs (1% decrease) (Figure 4C–D).
evidence: This claim is supported by scRNA-seq data analysis shown in Figure 4C-D.

claim: The top upregulated genes in aggregated mCherry-positive cells were also significant LRE cluster markers.
source: The top upregulated genes in aggregated mCherry-positive cells (ctsbb, lrp2b, ctsl.1, dab2, cpvl, cubn, tdo2b, lgmn, fabp6, sptbn5) were also significant LRE cluster markers (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by scRNA-seq data analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The most upregulated genes in aggregated mCherry-negative cells were also significant anterior enterocyte cluster markers.
source: On the other hand, the most upregulated genes in aggregated mCherry-negative cells (fabp2, chia.2, fabp1b.1, apobb.1, apoa4b.1, apoa1a, tm4sf4, afp4.1, apoc2, apoc1) were also significant anterior enterocyte cluster markers (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by scRNA-seq data analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Intact protein uptake in non-LRE cells is associated with the expression of a subset of markers involved in protein uptake in LREs.
source: These data suggest that intact protein uptake in non-LRE cells is associated with the expression of a subset of markers involved in protein uptake in LREs.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that mCherry-positive non-LRE cells express LRE markers.

claim: The lysosome pathway was strongly upregulated in anterior and posterior LREs in both GF and CV conditions.
source: For example, KEGG pathway analysis confirmed that the lysosome pathway was strongly upregulated in anterior and posterior LREs in both GF and CV conditions (Figure 5—figure supplement 1), distinguishing them from their closest cluster neighbors (Figure 5B, Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by KEGG pathway analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1 and Figure 5B.

claim: Both anterior and posterior LREs strongly expressed their characteristic endocytic machinery, composed of cubn, dab2, and amn.
source: In addition, both anterior and posterior LREs strongly expressed their characteristic endocytic machinery, composed of cubn, dab2, and amn (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by scRNA-seq data analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Bile salt transport genes fabp6 and slc10a2 were highly expressed in ileocytes, but expression also occurred in the LRE clusters at a gradient from anterior to posterior LREs.
source: Bile salt transport genes, fatty acid binding protein (fabp6), and solute carrier family 10 member 2 (slc10a2), were highly expressed in ileocytes, but expression also occurred in the LRE clusters at a gradient from anterior to posterior LREs (Figure 5C–D).
evidence: This claim is supported by scRNA-seq data analysis shown in Figure 5C-D.

claim: Tryptophan metabolism was a significantly upregulated KEGG pathway in anterior LREs in the GF and CV conditions.
source: Tryptophan metabolism was a significantly upregulated KEGG pathway in anterior LREs in the GF and CV conditions (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by KEGG pathway analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Expression of tryptophan metabolic genes kmo and tdo2a occurred in LREs and ileocytes.
source: Expression of tryptophan metabolic genes, including kynurenine 3-monoxygenase (kmo) and tryptophan 2,3-dioxygenase a (tdo2a), occurred in LREs and ileocytes (Figure 5D–E).
evidence: This claim is supported by scRNA-seq data analysis shown in Figure 5D-E.

claim: Anterior LREs showed high expression of tryptophan metabolic genes (tdo2b, aldh9a1a.1, kmo, tdo2a, ddc) in the GF and CV conditions.
source: Anterior LREs showed high expression of tryptophan metabolic genes (tdo2b, aldh9a1a.1, kmo, tdo2a, ddc) in the GF and CV conditions (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by scRNA-seq data analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Anterior and posterior LREs were distinguished by differential expression of several peptidases.
source: Furthermore, anterior and posterior LREs were distinguished by differential expression of several peptidases (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by scRNA-seq data analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Expression of several peptidase genes was higher in GF than in CV posterior LREs.
source: The differences between the GF and CV conditions were most apparent in posterior LREs where expression of several peptidase genes was higher in GF than in CV larvae (Figure 5F).
evidence: This claim is supported by scRNA-seq data analysis shown in Figure 5F.

claim: Cpvl is a serine carboxypeptidase predicted to localize to lysosomes.
source: Carboxypeptidase vitellogenic like (Cpvl), a serine carboxypeptidase, and Cathepsin La (Ctsla), a cysteine-type peptidase, are predicted to localized to lysosomes (Mahoney et al., 2001; Tingaud-Sequeira and Cerdà, 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Ctsla is a cysteine-type peptidase predicted to localize to lysosomes.
source: Carboxypeptidase vitellogenic like (Cpvl), a serine carboxypeptidase, and Cathepsin La (Ctsla), a cysteine-type peptidase, are predicted to localized to lysosomes (Mahoney et al., 2001; Tingaud-Sequeira and Cerdà, 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Pm20d1.2 is an amino acid hydrolase.
source: Peptidase M20 domain containing 1, tandem duplicate 2 (Pm20d1.2) is an amino acid hydrolase (Long et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Higher expression of protein-degradation genes cpvl, ctsla, and pm20d1.2 may contribute to the faster degradation rates observed in GF LREs.
source: These results raise the possibility that higher expression of protein-degradation genes cpvl, ctsla, and pm20d1.2 contributes to the faster degradation rates we observed in GF LREs.
evidence: This claim is speculative, connecting gene expression data to functional observations.

claim: In the CV condition, posterior LREs upregulated the expression of several genes involved in the immune response to bacteria.
source: In the CV condition, posterior LREs upregulated the expression of several genes involved in the immune response to bacteria (Figure 5G).
evidence: This claim is supported by scRNA-seq data analysis shown in Figure 5G.

claim: MyD88 signaling helps to prevent bacterial overgrowth and clears intestinal pathogens.
source: MyD88 signaling helps to prevent bacterial overgrowth and clears intestinal pathogens (van der Vaart et al., 2013; Karmarkar and Rock, 2013; Gibson et al., 2008; Franzenburg et al., 2012; van der Sar et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: MyD88 regulates expression of jund, a LPS-sensor that can induce inflammation in response to intestinal bacteria, including Aeromonas spp.
source: MyD88 also regulates expression of JunD proto-oncogene, AP-1 transcription factor subunit (jund), a LPS-sensor that can induce inflammation in response to the intestinal bacteria, including Aeromonas spp. (Meixner et al., 2004; Li et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: ehd1b is upregulated in response to bacterial infection and is involved in vesicle-mediated transport.
source: EH-domain containing 1b (ehd1b) is upregulated in response to bacterial infection and is involved in vesicle-mediated transport (Dubytska et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: The microbiome stimulates posterior LREs to upregulate expression of genes involved in directing the immune response to intestinal bacteria.
source: These patterns suggest that the microbiome stimulates posterior LREs to upregulate expression of genes involved in directing the immune response to intestinal bacteria.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that immune-related genes are upregulated in CV posterior LREs.

claim: The microbiome stimulated expression of dopamine synthesis and signaling genes in posterior LREs.
source: The microbiome also stimulated expression of dopamine synthesis and signaling genes in posterior LREs (Figure 5H).
evidence: This claim is supported by scRNA-seq data analysis shown in Figure 5H.

claim: ddc decarboxylates tryptophan to synthesize dopamine and serotonin.
source: These include dopamine decarboxylase (ddc), which decarboxylates tryptophan to synthesize dopamine and serotonin (Koyanagi et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: gnas is involved in the dopamine receptor signaling pathway.
source: Expression of GNAS complex locus (gnas), which is involved in the dopamine receptor signaling pathway (Lu et al., 2006; Vortherms et al., 2006), was also elevated in CV posterior LREs.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Posterior LREs were the only cell cluster in which gnas and ddc expression was significantly higher in the CV than GF condition.
source: Interestingly, posterior LREs were the only cell cluster in which gnas and ddc expression was significantly higher in the CV than GF condition.
evidence: This claim is supported by scRNA-seq data analysis.

claim: The gut microbiome increases dopamine synthesis and signaling pathways in posterior LREs.
source: These results suggest that the gut microbiome increases dopamine synthesis and signaling pathways in posterior LREs.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that dopamine-related genes are upregulated in CV posterior LREs.

claim: The microbiome upregulated several genes related to iron ion transport and homeostasis in LREs.
source: The microbiome also upregulated several genes related to iron ion transport and homeostasis in LREs (Figure 5I).
evidence: This claim is supported by scRNA-seq data analysis shown in Figure 5I.

claim: In the CV condition, posterior LREs cells had significantly elevated levels of slc11a2, slc40a1, and meltf.
source: In the CV condition, posterior LREs cells had significantly elevated levels of solute carrier family 11 member 2 (slc11a2), ferroportin (slc40a1), and melanotransferrin (meltf) (S5K).
evidence: This claim is supported by scRNA-seq data analysis.

claim: Anterior LRE cells showed increased expression of slc40a1 and meltf in the CV condition.
source: Anterior LRE cells also showed increased expression of slc40a1 and meltf (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by scRNA-seq data analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Slc11a2 helps regulate the influx of iron into the cell.
source: Slc11a2 helps regulate the influx of iron into the cell, while ferroportin regulates the export of iron out of the cell (Yilmaz and Li, 2018; Bao et al., 2024).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Ferroportin regulates the export of iron out of the cell.
source: Slc11a2 helps regulate the influx of iron into the cell, while ferroportin regulates the export of iron out of the cell (Yilmaz and Li, 2018; Bao et al., 2024).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Melanotransferrin has iron-binding properties and is predicted to localize to the plasma membrane, where it transports iron into the cell.
source: Melanotransferrin has iron-binding properties and is predicted to localize to the plasma membrane, where it transports iron into the cell (Sekyere et al., 2006; Dunn et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Melanotransferrin was an important cluster marker in Cloaca 3.
source: Interestingly, melanotransferrin was an important cluster marker in Cloaca 3, a cell cluster that only occurred in the CV condition and is directly adjacent to LREs in the intestine (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by scRNA-seq data analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Upregulation of iron transport genes is a consistent response to microbiome in LREs and other epithelial cells in the distal intestine.
source: These results suggest that upregulation of iron transport genes is a consistent response to microbiome in LREs and other epithelial cells in the distal intestine.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that iron transport genes are upregulated in multiple cell types in CV conditions.

claim: LREs upregulate genes in response to microbial colonization that are involved in innate immunity, iron homeostasis, and dopamine-synthesis and signaling pathways.
source: Together, these scRNA-seq data revealed that LREs upregulate genes in response to microbial colonization that are involved in innate immunity, iron homeostasis, and dopamine-synthesis and signaling pathways, and they downregulate several peptidases that may linked to reduced protein degradation upon microbial colonization.
evidence: This claim synthesizes multiple findings from scRNA-seq data analysis.

claim: LREs downregulate several peptidases upon microbial colonization that may be linked to reduced protein degradation.
source: Together, these scRNA-seq data revealed that LREs upregulate genes in response to microbial colonization that are involved in innate immunity, iron homeostasis, and dopamine-synthesis and signaling pathways, and they downregulate several peptidases that may linked to reduced protein degradation upon microbial colonization.
evidence: This claim synthesizes findings from scRNA-seq data and connects them to functional observations.

claim: A. calcoaceticus may be classified as an anti-inflammatory bacterial strain because it reduces intestinal neutrophil recruitment.
source: A. calcoaceticus may be classified as an anti-inflammatory bacterial strain because it reduces intestinal neutrophil recruitment (Rolig et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Colonization with A. calcoaceticus only mildly reduced protein uptake activity.
source: Colonization with A. calcoaceticus only mildly reduced protein uptake activity, and it did not reduce expression of endocytic machinery.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from monoassociation experiments.

claim: A. calcoaceticus colonization did not reduce expression of endocytic machinery.
source: Colonization with A. calcoaceticus only mildly reduced protein uptake activity, and it did not reduce expression of endocytic machinery.
evidence: This claim is supported by HCR data from monoassociation experiments.

claim: V. cholerae and A. caviae are pro-inflammatory strains.
source: In contrast, the pro-inflammatory strains, V. cholerae and A. caviae (Rolig et al., 2015), reduced LRE activity and endocytic expression.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: V. cholerae and A. caviae reduced LRE activity and endocytic expression.
source: In contrast, the pro-inflammatory strains, V. cholerae and A. caviae (Rolig et al., 2015), reduced LRE activity and endocytic expression.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from monoassociation experiments.

claim: V. cholerae colonization causes intestinal neutrophil recruitment and stimulates macrophages to express TNF-alpha.
source: V. cholerae colonization causes intestinal neutrophil recruitment and stimulates macrophages to express TNF-alpha (Wiles et al., 2020; Ngo et al., 2024).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The V. cholerae strain used in this study does not encode cholera toxin or toxin-coregulated pilus.
source: Importantly, the V. cholerae strain we used here does not encode cholera toxin or toxin-coregulated pilus (Stephens et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research characterizing the bacterial strain.

claim: V. cholerae has been shown to increase intestinal contractility in zebrafish.
source: This strain has been shown to increase intestinal contractility in zebrafish (Ngo, Amitabh, Ngo et al., 2024) and may affect protein absorption under nutrient limiting conditions.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: LP-fed cubn mutants developed a distinct microbiome community with diminished species richness.
source: Our investigations into the impact of LRE protein uptake activity on the gut microbiome revealed diet-dependent effects on the microbial community. LP-fed, cubn mutants developed a distinct microbiome community with diminished species richness.
evidence: This claim is supported by 16S rRNA gene sequencing data.

claim: Aeromonas was the only genus that proliferated in cubn mutants compared to heterozygotes.
source: Aeromonas was the only genus that proliferated in cubn mutants compared to heterozygotes.
evidence: This claim is supported by 16S rRNA gene sequencing data.

claim: Aeromonas is considered a part of the core zebrafish gut microbiome.
source: While Aeromonas is considered a part of the core zebrafish gut microbiome (Roeselers et al., 2011), some species are inflammatory (Rolig et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Some Aeromonas species are inflammatory.
source: While Aeromonas is considered a part of the core zebrafish gut microbiome (Roeselers et al., 2011), some species are inflammatory (Rolig et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: A. caviae can reduce LRE protein uptake activity.
source: As discussed, A. caviae can reduce LRE protein uptake activity.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from monoassociation experiments presented earlier in the manuscript.

claim: Host protein deprivation through impaired LRE activity may lead to proliferation of proinflammatory bacteria like Aeromonas that can further reduce protein uptake activity by LREs.
source: This result suggests that host protein deprivation through the impaired LRE activity may lead to proliferation of proinflammatory bacteria like Aeromonas that can further reduce protein uptake activity by LREs.
evidence: This claim is speculative, connecting multiple observations to propose a mechanism.

claim: mCherry uptake was reduced by A. calcoaceticus monoassociation.
source: mCherry uptake was reduced by A. calcoaceticus (two-way ANOVA, p=0.0268, n=19–20), P. mendocina (two-way ANOVA, p=0.0033, n=20–21), A. caviae (two-way ANOVA,p<0.0001, n=19–20) and V. cholerae (two-way ANOVA, p<0.0001, n=18–20).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis from monoassociation experiments.

claim: mCherry uptake was reduced by P. mendocina monoassociation.
source: mCherry uptake was reduced by A. calcoaceticus (two-way ANOVA, p=0.0268, n=19–20), P. mendocina (two-way ANOVA, p=0.0033, n=20–21), A. caviae (two-way ANOVA,p<0.0001, n=19–20) and V. cholerae (two-way ANOVA, p<0.0001, n=18–20).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis from monoassociation experiments.

claim: mCherry uptake was reduced by A. caviae monoassociation.
source: mCherry uptake was reduced by A. calcoaceticus (two-way ANOVA, p=0.0268, n=19–20), P. mendocina (two-way ANOVA, p=0.0033, n=20–21), A. caviae (two-way ANOVA,p<0.0001, n=19–20) and V. cholerae (two-way ANOVA, p<0.0001, n=18–20).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis from monoassociation experiments.

claim: mCherry uptake was reduced by V. cholerae monoassociation.
source: mCherry uptake was reduced by A. calcoaceticus (two-way ANOVA, p=0.0268, n=19–20), P. mendocina (two-way ANOVA, p=0.0033, n=20–21), A. caviae (two-way ANOVA,p<0.0001, n=19–20) and V. cholerae (two-way ANOVA, p<0.0001, n=18–20).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis from monoassociation experiments.

claim: GF larvae had significantly higher levels of dab2 expression than those colonized with V. cholerae.
source: By comparing the integrated signal obtained from max projection of confocal stacks, we found that GF larvae had significantly higher levels of dab2 expression than those colonized with V. cholerae (Figure 6D).
evidence: This claim is supported by HCR data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 6D.

claim: V. cholerae significantly reduced cubn expression.
source: We found that while V. cholerae significantly reduced cubn expression, A. calcoaceticus did not (Figure 6F).
evidence: This claim is supported by HCR data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 6F.

claim: A. calcoaceticus did not significantly reduce cubn expression.
source: We found that while V. cholerae significantly reduced cubn expression, A. calcoaceticus did not (Figure 6F).
evidence: This claim is supported by HCR data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 6F.

claim: V. cholerae reduced expression of ctsh compared to GF larvae.
source: We found that V. cholerae reduced expression of ctsh and ctsz compared to A. calcoaceticus and GF larvae, which presented similar levels of ctsz expression (Figure 6G-H).
evidence: This claim is supported by HCR data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 6G.

claim: V. cholerae reduced expression of ctsz compared to GF larvae.
source: We found that V. cholerae reduced expression of ctsh and ctsz compared to A. calcoaceticus and GF larvae, which presented similar levels of ctsz expression (Figure 6G-H).
evidence: This claim is supported by HCR data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 6H.

claim: A. calcoaceticus and GF larvae presented similar levels of ctsz expression.
source: We found that V. cholerae reduced expression of ctsh and ctsz compared to A. calcoaceticus and GF larvae, which presented similar levels of ctsz expression (Figure 6G-H).
evidence: This claim is supported by HCR data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 6H.

claim: Microbial colonization reduces both protein uptake and degradation in LREs by modulating the expression of endocytic and lysosomal proteins.
source: Together, our data reveal that microbial colonization reduces both protein uptake and degradation in LREs by modulating the expression of endocytic and lysosomal proteins.
evidence: This claim synthesizes multiple experimental findings.

claim: Diet strongly affected microbiome composition in heterozygotes.
source: Diet strongly affected microbiome composition in heterozygotes (Bray Curtis distance, p=0.001), but not in cubn homozygous mutants (Bray Curtis distance, p=0.18) (Figure 7B–C).
evidence: This claim is supported by 16S rRNA gene sequencing data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 7B-C.

claim: Diet did not strongly affect microbiome composition in cubn homozygous mutants.
source: Diet strongly affected microbiome composition in heterozygotes (Bray Curtis distance, p=0.001), but not in cubn homozygous mutants (Bray Curtis distance, p=0.18) (Figure 7B–C).
evidence: This claim is supported by 16S rRNA gene sequencing data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 7B-C.

claim: Mutants had significantly different microbiomes than heterozygotes when they were fed a LP diet.
source: Mutants had significantly different microbiomes than heterozygotes when they were fed a LP diet (Bray Curtis distance, p=0.023), but not a HP diet (Bray Curtis distance, p=0.34) (Figure 7B–C).
evidence: This claim is supported by 16S rRNA gene sequencing data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 7B-C.

claim: Mutants did not have significantly different microbiomes than heterozygotes when they were fed a HP diet.
source: Mutants had significantly different microbiomes than heterozygotes when they were fed a LP diet (Bray Curtis distance, p=0.023), but not a HP diet (Bray Curtis distance, p=0.34) (Figure 7B–C).
evidence: This claim is supported by 16S rRNA gene sequencing data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 7B-C.

claim: LP-fed cubn mutants had significantly lower microbial richness than HP-fed mutants.
source: LP-fed cubn mutants had significantly lower microbial richness than HP-fed mutants (Two-tailed t-test, p=0.0094, n=6–9).
evidence: This claim is supported by 16S rRNA gene sequencing data and statistical analysis.

claim: The combination of the LP-diet and cubn mutation lowers taxa richness and affects the mutant microbiome.
source: These results suggest that the combination of the LP-diet and cubn mutation lowers taxa richness and affects the mutant microbiome.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the 16S rRNA gene sequencing data.

claim: Gammaproteobacteria were significantly more abundant in HP than LP-fed heterozygotes.
source: Gammaproteobacteria were significantly more abundant in HP than LP-fed heterozygotes (DESeq2, padj = 0.02).
evidence: This claim is supported by 16S rRNA gene sequencing data and statistical analysis.

claim: LP-fed mutants were deficient in Alphaproteobacteria, which were more abundant in LP-fed heterozygotes.
source: LP-fed mutants were deficient in Alphaproteobacteria, which were more abundant in LP-fed heterozygotes (DESeq2, padj = 0.021) (Figure 7E).
evidence: This claim is supported by 16S rRNA gene sequencing data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 7E.

claim: Mutants consistently had fewer differentially abundant taxa than heterozygotes at the class and genus levels.
source: Indeed, one important trend was that mutants consistently had fewer differentially abundant taxa than heterozygotes at the class and genus levels (Figure 7F).
evidence: This claim is supported by 16S rRNA gene sequencing data analysis shown in Figure 7F.

claim: Pseudomonas spp. were significantly more abundant in HP than LP-fed heterozygotes.
source: Pseudomonas spp. were significantly more abundant in HP than LP-fed heterozygotes (DESeq2, padj = 0.002) (Figure 7G).
evidence: This claim is supported by 16S rRNA gene sequencing data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 7G.

claim: Hassalia was significantly more abundant in LP-fed mutants than in heterozygotes.
source: One genus, Hassalia, was significantly more abundant in LP-fed mutants than in heterozygotes (DESeq2, padj = 6.04E-21).
evidence: This claim is supported by 16S rRNA gene sequencing data and statistical analysis.

claim: Aeromonas spp. were more highly abundant in cubn mutants than heterozygotes independently of diet.
source: Independently of diet, Aeromonas spp. were more highly abundant in cubn mutants than heterozygotes (DESeq2, padj = 0.01) (Figure 7H).
evidence: This claim is supported by 16S rRNA gene sequencing data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 7H.

claim: LRE activity and dietary protein content can interactively affect the larval zebrafish microbiome.
source: Together, these results suggest that LRE activity and dietary protein content can interactively affect the larval zebrafish microbiome.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the 16S rRNA gene sequencing data showing interactive effects.

claim: The cubn mutation may lead to the proliferation of certain microbes that can reduce protein uptake activity in LREs.
source: Furthermore, the cubn mutation may lead to the proliferation of certain microbes that can reduce protein uptake activity in LREs.
evidence: This claim is speculative, connecting observations about Aeromonas abundance in mutants with its effects on LRE activity.

claim: The gut microbiome reduces the rates of protein uptake and degradation in LREs and reduces expression of lysosomal protease genes.
source: The results of our investigations reveal reciprocal interactions between LREs and the gut microbiome that impact host nutrition. We show that the gut microbiome slows the rates of protein uptake and degradation in LREs and reduces expression of lysosomal protease genes.
evidence: This claim synthesizes multiple experimental findings from the study.

claim: Monoassociated bacteria such as Aeromonas caviae and Vibrio cholerae reduce protein uptake in LREs and downregulate expression of endocytic and protease genes.
source: We also found that monoassociated bacteria such as Aeromonas caviae and Vibrio cholerae reduce protein uptake in LREs and downregulate expression of endocytic and protease genes.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from monoassociation experiments.

claim: Impaired LRE protein uptake activity and dietary protein content impact the microbiome.
source: Finally, we show that impaired LRE protein uptake activity and dietary protein content impact the microbiome.
evidence: This claim is supported by 16S rRNA gene sequencing data.

claim: The microbe-dependent downregulation of protein uptake may limit the transepithelial transport of microbial products, thus dampening the expression of pro-inflammatory markers.
source: One possibility is that this effect limits the transepithelial transport of microbial products, which occurs as a byproduct of the endocytic activity of LREs, thus dampening the expression of pro-inflammatory markers.
evidence: This claim is speculative, proposing a possible mechanism for the observed effects.

claim: Microbial suppression of absorptive gene expression programs across enterocyte populations may be a broader conserved theme in intestinal physiology.
source: This suggests that microbial inhibition of absorptive gene expression programs across enterocyte populations may be a broader conserved theme in intestinal physiology.
evidence: This claim is inferred by comparing findings from this study with prior research on lipid absorption.

claim: Tryptophan metabolites, including kynurenine derivatives, are AhR receptor ligands that downregulate host immune response to bacterial antigens.
source: Tryptophan metabolites, including kynurenine derivatives, are AhR receptor ligands that downregulate host immune response to bacterial antigens (Bessede et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Tryptophan metabolic activity in LREs could participate in host tolerance of the gut microbiome.
source: These results suggest that tryptophan metabolic activity in LREs could participate in host tolerance of the gut microbiome, and inflammation may affect protein uptake activity in LREs.
evidence: This claim is speculative, proposing a possible role for tryptophan metabolism based on gene expression data.

claim: Inflammation may affect protein uptake activity in LREs.
source: These results suggest that tryptophan metabolic activity in LREs could participate in host tolerance of the gut microbiome, and inflammation may affect protein uptake activity in LREs.
evidence: This claim is speculative, proposing a possible mechanism based on observed gene expression patterns.

claim: The microbiome increases intestinal iron absorption.
source: The microbiome increases intestinal iron absorption (Mayneris-Perxachs et al., 2022), but its effect on iron absorption in LREs is unknown.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Host iron nutrition and luminal iron levels can affect the gut microbiome community and proliferation of microbial pathogens.
source: Host iron nutrition and luminal iron levels can affect the gut microbiome community and proliferation of microbial pathogens (Mayneris-Perxachs et al., 2022; Dostal et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Iron absorption and secretion by LREs may affect the gut microbiome community and play a role in host-microbiome homeostasis.
source: Iron absorption and secretion by LREs may affect the gut microbiome community and play a role in host-microbiome homeostasis.
evidence: This claim is speculative, proposing a possible role for LRE iron transport based on gene expression data.

claim: V. cholerae monoassociation did not significantly affect fish growth.
source: V. cholerae monoassociation did not significantly affect fish growth (Two-tailed t-test, p=0.66, n=18–22) (Figure 6—figure supplement 1), suggesting that interactions with LREs rather than systemic effects reduced uptake activity.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Interactions with LREs rather than systemic effects reduced uptake activity in V. cholerae-colonized larvae.
source: V. cholerae monoassociation did not significantly affect fish growth (Two-tailed t-test, p=0.66, n=18–22) (Figure 6—figure supplement 1), suggesting that interactions with LREs rather than systemic effects reduced uptake activity.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that V. cholerae affects LRE activity without affecting overall growth.

claim: There was no difference in mCherry uptake between larvae initially gavaged with live V. cholerae or PBS.
source: Interestingly, there was no difference in mCherry uptake between larvae that were initially gavaged with live V. cholerae or PBS (Figure 6—figure supplement 1), indicating that longer-term exposure to V. cholerae is required to reduce protein uptake activity in LREs.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Longer-term exposure to V. cholerae is required to reduce protein uptake activity in LREs.
source: Interestingly, there was no difference in mCherry uptake between larvae that were initially gavaged with live V. cholerae or PBS (Figure 6—figure supplement 1), indicating that longer-term exposure to V. cholerae is required to reduce protein uptake activity in LREs.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental data showing no acute effect of V. cholerae on LRE uptake.

claim: There was no difference in pronephros mCherry signal between GF, CV, and V. cholerae-monoassociated larvae.
source: There was no difference in pronephros signal between these conditions, indicating that intestinal microbes were not causing LREs to increase mCherry trans-epithelial transport through transcytosis (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Intestinal microbes were not causing LREs to increase mCherry trans-epithelial transport through transcytosis.
source: There was no difference in pronephros signal between these conditions, indicating that intestinal microbes were not causing LREs to increase mCherry trans-epithelial transport through transcytosis (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental data showing no difference in pronephros signal.

claim: Luminal mCherry concentration was the same in GF and V. cholerae-colonized larvae at 1 hr PG.
source: The concentration was the same in both conditions (Figure 6—figure supplement 1), showing that V. cholerae does not significantly reduce mCherry concentrations in the intestinal lumen within these timeframes.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: V. cholerae does not significantly reduce mCherry concentrations in the intestinal lumen within these timeframes.
source: The concentration was the same in both conditions (Figure 6—figure supplement 1), showing that V. cholerae does not significantly reduce mCherry concentrations in the intestinal lumen within these timeframes.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental data showing similar luminal mCherry concentrations.
